prompt: Write a short blog post about the first harvest of the year. Aim for about 400 words. Reply with the post only.
final_message:
# The First Harvest

There's a particular kind of quiet that settles over the garden in early summer. The seeds are in, the seedlings are staked, and all you can do is wait. Then one morning you walk out with your coffee and notice something red hiding under a leaf.

This year, the first harvest came earlier than I expected. It wasn't a basket overflowing with produce. It was a handful of radishes, a few leaves of lettuce, and a single, slightly lopsided strawberry. But I'll remember it longer than I'll remember the bigger hauls to come.

## The Radishes

Radishes are the garden's way of encouraging beginners. They sprout in days and ask for almost nothing. I pulled the first one with more ceremony than it deserved, brushing off the soil with my thumb to reveal a bright pink globe. I rinsed it under the hose, took a bite right there in the yard, and was met with a crisp, peppery snap. Nothing from a grocery store has ever tasted quite like that.

## The Lettuce

The lettuce had been quietly thriving in the shade of the taller plants. I snipped the outer leaves with kitchen scissors, leaving the center to keep growing. That's the trick I learned last year: take a little at a time, and the plant keeps giving. By evening I'd made a salad of tender greens with olive oil, lemon, and a pinch of salt. It was simple, and it was perfect.

## The Strawberry

Then there was the strawberry. I had been checking on it daily, watching it go from green to white to blushing pink. I nearly picked it too soon, but patience won out. When I finally plucked it, warm from the sun, I split it with my partner. One berry, two bites. It was sweeter than anything I could have bought, mostly because I had watched it every step of the way.

## What It Teaches You

A first harvest is a lesson in slowing down. Gardening runs on the plants' schedule, not mine. There are weeks of watering, weeding, worrying about frost, and wondering whether anything will come up at all. And then, without fanfare, the reward arrives, small and generous.

I've also learned not to measure success by volume. The tomatoes, zucchini, and beans will come soon enough, and I'll probably be giving bags of them to the neighbors. But the first harvest is different. It's proof that the effort was worth it, and a promise of more to come.

So if you're thinking about starting a garden, start small. Plant some radishes. Be patient. And when that first bite arrives, eat it right there in the dirt, with your hands still muddy.

You'll understand.
